claims.text: The multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy forms a protective oxide or passive film at elevated temperature.
The protective film forms on distinct constituent phases of the eutectic alloy.
Mechanical wear disrupts or removes the protective oxide film.
Film removal repeatedly exposes less-corrosion-resistant substrate regions.
The newly exposed substrate regions corrode more rapidly.
Corrosion of the exposed substrate compromises subsequent formation or maintenance of the passive barrier.
Wear-induced film breakdown and corrosion form a positive feedback loop.
The eutectic alloy has a finely distributed eutectic microstructure.
The elevated-temperature passive film is thermally unstable.
Increasing temperature promotes defect formation, including oxygen vacancies, in passive films and affects chloride transport.
Temperature-induced defects in the oxide accelerate electrochemical degradation of the exposed phases.
Under simultaneous wear and corrosion, total degradation will significantly exceed the sum of isolated wear-only and corrosion-only degradation.
Simultaneous exposure will increase the wear rate because film removal exposes softer, corroded material.
Simultaneous exposure will increase the corrosion rate because wear continuously exposes reactive substrate.
Both wear and corrosion rates will be higher than in a matched monophase alloy.
The matched monophase alloy lacks the eutectic alloy's two-phase protective-film behavior.
A temperature above 600°C and a chloride-containing sulfuric-acid medium are relevant boundary conditions for the proposed coupled degradation mechanism.
Changing chloride concentration should modulate the coupled degradation rate.

contradictions.description: The boundary requires identical mechanical loads across all comparisons, but the corrosion-only condition must have no mechanical wear load to remain a corrosion-only control. Loads can be matched between wear-only and combined tests, but not across all three conditions.
